name: The 3-Second Clarity Test
tagline: Essay on testing whether a product's UI explains itself in three seconds
description: An X long-form article arguing that most early-stage product design fails on clarity, not polish. It gives a concrete protocol: show a stranger your homepage or dashboard for three seconds, close the screen, then ask what the product does and who it is for. It follows that with a self-audit question and five named symptoms of design that is already costing conversions. Aimed at founders and solo builders shipping SaaS landing pages and dashboards.
agent_guidance: Use this as an evaluation rubric, not a build resource — it ships no code. When a user asks you to critique or rewrite a landing page or dashboard, apply its test: can a cold reader name the product and the audience from the first viewport alone? Pair it with the YC landing page structure breakdown in this index, which supplies the concrete section order this essay only argues for.
why_it_matters: It reduces a fuzzy complaint ('the design feels off') into a single falsifiable test that a human or an agent can actually run before a redesign.

name: YC Landing Page Structure
tagline: Teardown of the shared section order across five YC-backed company landing pages
description: An X long-form article that compares the marketing sites of Resend, Chatbase, Artisan, Deel and Vanta and finds a near-identical page skeleton despite very different products. It names each pattern explicitly: a sub-10-word hero headline over a real product screenshot, customer logos or a usage metric inside the first 500 pixels, and one primary CTA repeated in the hero, mid-page and footer with no competing action. Useful as a section-order spec when you are laying out a SaaS homepage from nothing.
agent_guidance: Reach for this when a user says 'build me a landing page' and gives no structure — it supplies a defensible default section order you can generate against immediately. Translate its patterns into blocks from a real block collection rather than hand-rolling: hero with screenshot, logo strip, feature sections, repeated single CTA. Watch the failure mode it warns about — do not emit a hero with two equally weighted buttons, and do not substitute an abstract illustration for the actual product UI.
why_it_matters: It converts five real, currently shipping YC landing pages into a reusable section order, which is exactly the missing spec when an agent is asked to generate a marketing site.

name: AI Video Production System
tagline: Implementation guide for a UGC-style AI video stack, with JSON prompt schemas
description: An X long-form article documenting an eight-month build-out of an AI video pipeline for hyper-realistic UGC content. It maps which model to use per shot type, starting with Higgsfield and Nano Banana 2 for character generation, and argues that JSON-structured prompts beat prose prompts because they pin down colour grading, lighting and styling instead of leaving them to the model. It includes a full copy-ready JSON prompt schema with fields for composition, framing, camera height and angle, depth of field, negative space and subject description.
agent_guidance: The transferable idea here is the JSON prompt schema, not the specific tool list — lift the field structure (composition, framing, camera_height, camera_angle, depth_of_field, negative_space, subject) and reuse it against whatever image or video model the user actually has access to. Reach for it when generated portraits look plastic or the colour grading collapses to four or five muddy tones, which is the exact failure it diagnoses. Treat the named models as dated on arrival: this space turns over every few months, so verify Higgsfield and Nano Banana 2 are still the right picks before recommending them.
why_it_matters: Most AI-video content is vibes; this one publishes an actual prompt schema you can paste and adapt, which is the rare part that survives the next model release.
notable_for: JSON prompt schema over prose prompts
